title: Risk Is Not the Same as Test Coverage
slack_text:
🧪 *QE Daily #001 — Risk Is Not the Same as Test Coverage*

*What is it?*
High test coverage does not automatically mean high risk coverage. A feature can have dozens of test cases and still leave the most damaging failure modes barely exercised.

*Why QA/QE should care*
A QE should prioritise based on impact, likelihood, detectability, change surface, dependencies and recoverability — not simply the number of scenarios written.

*Hypothetical scenario*
A travel app changes the traveller-selection component. The team validates many UI combinations, but the same component feeds pricing, fare eligibility and downstream booking requests.

*Think like a QE*
Ask: Which failures could produce the largest customer or business impact? Which integrations changed? What could silently return plausible-but-wrong data?

*Challenge*
You only have 45 minutes before release. Would you spend it executing 20 low-risk UI permutations or 5 tests around traveller counts, pricing and booking payloads? What evidence would change your choice?

*Takeaway*
Coverage tells you what you tested. Risk analysis tells you what matters most.

💬 Reply in the thread with how you would prioritise the 45 minutes.
thread_answer: A stronger approach is to rank the changed behaviour by impact and failure propagation. Start with traveller combinations that alter pricing or booking payloads, inspect the network request, verify pricing consistency across search/result/booking boundaries, then use remaining time for representative UI permutations. The exact choice should depend on evidence such as code-change scope, incident history, dependency changes and production observability.
linkedin_text:
QE Daily #001 — Risk is not the same as test coverage.

A feature can have 50 test cases and still be poorly tested if the highest-impact failures sit outside those 50.

Consider a traveller-selection change in a travel product. It is easy to spend most of the test effort checking UI combinations. But traveller counts may also influence pricing, fare eligibility, request payloads and downstream booking behaviour.

The Quality Engineering question is not simply, ‘How many scenarios did we execute?’

It is: ‘Which failures matter most, how likely are they, how far can they propagate, and what evidence would tell us we are safe to release?’

When time is constrained, I would rather execute a smaller number of high-value tests around pricing and booking boundaries than maximise a raw test-case count.

Coverage tells us what we tested. Risk analysis tells us what deserves attention first.

How do you decide what not to test when release time is limited?
